claims.text: Severe lattice distortion arising from atomic size mismatch is the primary mechanism governing strength and deformation in multi-component concentrated alloys.
Atomic size mismatch generates local lattice strain fields.
Lattice distortion impedes dislocation motion through local shear-modulus variations.
Enhanced lattice distortion increases the energy barrier for dislocation nucleation.
Enhanced lattice distortion increases the energy barrier for dislocation motion.
Increasing atomic-size differences among alloy constituents increases yield stress.
Partially substituting an alloying element with one closer in atomic size to the majority constituents will reduce lattice distortion.
Reducing lattice distortion makes dislocation motion less impeded.
The reduced-size-mismatch variant will have lower yield strength than the baseline equiatomic alloy.
The reduced-size-mismatch variant will have a modified work-hardening exponent relative to the baseline.
The hypothesis is expected to apply while the alloys remain single-phase solid solutions and diffusion-induced relaxation or secondary-phase precipitation does not dominate their mechanical response.
Short-range order and nanoscale precipitation may provide strengthening effects that are difficult to decouple from lattice distortion.
A lack of statistically significant yield-strength reduction or work-hardening change after reducing size mismatch would falsify the proposed governing role of lattice distortion.
Similar dislocation pinning in the baseline and reduced-mismatch alloys would falsify the proposed mechanism.
